unitTitle: Unit 1.0: Self-Exploration, Happiness & Prosperity
prompt: What is self-exploration? Explain its process.
modelAnswer:
Self-exploration is the process of dialogue between "what I am" (my present beliefs, desires, behaviour) and "what I really want to be" (my natural acceptance).
• I first observe my own conditioning – my beliefs, assumptions and behaviour as they are today.
• I then check them against my natural acceptance – what is naturally acceptable to me, e.g. trust, respect, happiness.
• The proposal is then verified by living (experiential validation) – does it give lasting happiness in actual life?
• What is found true is adopted; what is false is dropped. This brings continuous self-correction.
• It is a self-driven, universal and verifiable process – nothing is to be accepted just because someone said so.
markingScheme: 2M: I first observe my own conditioning
2M: I then check them against my natural acceptance
1M: It is a self-driven, universal and verifiable process

unitTitle: Unit 1.0: Self-Exploration, Happiness & Prosperity
prompt: Explain natural acceptance and experiential validation.
modelAnswer:
• Natural acceptance: the feeling that is naturally acceptable to every human being without any conditioning – e.g. everybody wants to be respected, trusted, happy.
• Experiential validation: checking a proposal by actually living it and observing its result in my life, family and surroundings.
• Natural acceptance is the first test; experiential validation is the second test. A proposal is accepted only when both agree.
• Natural acceptance does not change with time, place or person, whereas conditioned beliefs keep changing.
[Point | Natural acceptance | Experiential validation]
• Nature | Inner feeling / acceptance | Living and verifying
• Based on | Self (I) | Experience in life
• Role | Tells "what is right" for me | Confirms it in practice

unitTitle: Unit 1.0: Self-Exploration, Happiness & Prosperity
prompt: Explain the basic guidelines for value education.
modelAnswer:
Value education must satisfy four basic guidelines so that it is acceptable to all:
• Universality – the content must be true for all human beings, at all times and places.
• Rationality – it must be understandable and logical, to be accepted by reasoning.
• Naturalness – it must be naturally acceptable to the Self, without pressure or fear.
• Verifiability – it can be verified by every person on the basis of his/her own living (experiential validation).
• Together they make the content "all-encompassing and leading to harmony".

unitTitle: Unit 1.0: Self-Exploration, Happiness & Prosperity
prompt: What is value education? Explain its need, content, process and the basic guidelines.
modelAnswer:
1. Meaning
• Value education is the education that helps us understand what is of value to us and how to live in harmony – within ourselves, with family, society and nature.
• It complements skills (how to do) with values (what to do and why).
2. Need for value education
• Technology and skills have grown, but happiness and peace have not – the result is stress, depression, family breakdown, terrorism, pollution and global warming.
• Skills without values can be misused – e.g. technology for weapons or exploitation of nature.
• It gives a correct understanding of what we really want (happiness and prosperity) and how to achieve it.
• It helps us set our goals and priorities right and remove confusion and contradiction in our thinking.
3. Content of value education
• Understanding the basic human aspirations – happiness and prosperity.
• Understanding human being as co-existence of Self and Body.
• Understanding harmony at four levels: individual, family, society, nature/existence.
• Understanding values in human relationships and ethical conduct.
4. Process of value education
• The process is self-exploration: natural acceptance + experiential validation.
• Not by memorising or accepting on authority, but by verifying within oneself.
5. Basic guidelines
• Universality, Rationality, Naturalness, Verifiability.
Conclusion
• Value education makes us aware of what is right and enables us to live with continuous happiness and mutual prosperity.

modelAnswer:

unitTitle: Unit 1.0: Self-Exploration, Happiness & Prosperity
prompt: Why do we not have continuous happiness today even though physical facilities have increased?
modelAnswer:
• We assume physical facility = happiness, which is a wrong assumption.
• Physical facility gives only temporary pleasure to the body; its effect ends when the facility is used up.
• The desire for more is unlimited, so there is a permanent feeling of deprivation.
• The Self (I) needs happiness through right understanding and relationship, which we ignore.
• Result – stress, loneliness, broken relationships and nature exploitation despite plenty of facilities.

unitTitle: Unit 1.0: Self-Exploration, Happiness & Prosperity
prompt: Explain the method to fulfil the basic human aspirations.
modelAnswer:
• Step 1: Understand the aspirations – happiness and prosperity – and what is required for each.
• Step 2: Right understanding (of oneself, relationships and existence) comes first.
• Step 3: Live in right relationship with trust and respect.
• Step 4: Assess the need for physical facility correctly and produce/earn it with labour.
• Result: continuous happiness (through understanding + relationship) and prosperity (through physical facility).

unitTitle: Unit 1.0: Self-Exploration, Happiness & Prosperity
prompt: Explain the basic human aspirations – happiness and prosperity. Discuss the current scenario about their fulfilment and the way to fulfil them continuously.
modelAnswer:
1. Basic human aspirations
• Every human being wants to live with happiness (a state of harmony) and prosperity (sufficiency of physical facility).
• These are common to all, irrespective of age, place, religion or profession – hence "basic".
• We want them continuously, not for a moment or a day.
2. Current scenario
• We are trying to fulfil both through accumulation of physical facility only.
• The individual level: stress, depression, anxiety, suicide. Family level: breakdown of relationships, dowry, divorce, generation gap.
• Society level: terrorism, communal violence, corruption, wars, disparities. Nature level: pollution, global warming, resource depletion.
• Result: people have more facilities but less happiness and a feeling of insecurity and deprivation.
3. Why this happens
• Wrong assumption that physical facility = happiness.
• Ignoring the need of the Self (happiness) and focusing only on the need of the Body (facility).
• No assessment of need, so desire for more is unlimited.
4. The way to fulfil them
• Develop right understanding through self-exploration.
• Live in right relationships based on trust and respect.
• Make physical facilities available in the right quantity through proper work.
• Make others also happy – mutual happiness and mutual prosperity.
Conclusion
• Continuous happiness is possible only by harmony of right understanding, relationship and physical facility in the right order.

prompt: What is right understanding? Explain its need and how its lack creates problems at the individual, family, society and nature levels.
modelAnswer:

2. Need

• To remove contradictions in values, beliefs and behaviour.
• To decide priorities correctly – understanding first, relationship second, physical facility third.
3. Effects of lack of right understanding
• Individual: stress, depression, inferiority, suicidal thoughts.
• Family: distrust, conflicts, divorce, generation gap.
• Society: violence, terrorism, corruption, exploitation, communalism.
• Nature: pollution, climate change, over-consumption, loss of biodiversity.
4. How to develop right understanding
• Through self-exploration: natural acceptance + experiential validation.
• Through value education and a fair, supportive environment (family, institution, society).
• By living what is understood – sanskar.
Conclusion
• Right understanding is the root; once it is in place, relationship and physical facility start working in harmony, and happiness becomes continuous.

unitTitle: Unit 2.0: Relationship, Physical Facility & Human Being
topicTitle: Right Understanding, Relationship and Physical Facility
prompt: Explain right understanding, relationship and physical facility as the three requirements for fulfilling human aspirations. Why must they follow the correct sequence?
modelAnswer:
1. Introduction
• Human aspirations are happiness and prosperity. Three things are required: right understanding, relationship and physical facility.
2. Right understanding
• Understanding of what is real, what is to be done and what is beneficial. It is the foundation.
• Needed continuously, by every human being, at all times.
3. Relationship
• Living with others on the basis of trust, respect, affection and care.
• It brings the feeling of mutual happiness; the need is continuous because humans live in relationships.
4. Physical facility
• Food, clothing, shelter, medicine, transport, etc. – required for the nourishment, protection and right utilisation of the Body.
• The need is limited and quantifiable; excess is a burden.
5. Why the sequence matters
• If understanding is missing, we assume facility = happiness and run after it endlessly.
• Facility without relationship becomes conflict and exploitation.
• With the right sequence, facilities are used for mutual prosperity and relationships for mutual happiness.
Example
• A rich family with no trust among members is still unhappy; a modest family with trust and respect is happy – showing that relationship and understanding matter more.
Conclusion
• Hence we must follow understanding → relationship → physical facility to get both happiness and prosperity.

unitTitle: Unit 2.0: Relationship, Physical Facility & Human Being
topicTitle: Human Being as Co-existence of the Sentient 'Self' and the Material 'Body'
prompt: Explain the human being as the co-existence of the sentient 'Self' and the material 'Body'. Differentiate their characteristics and needs.
modelAnswer:
1. Introduction
• A human being is not just a Body. It is the co-existence of the Self (I) and the Body, which constantly interact.
2. The Self ('I')
• Sentient / conscious; the seer, doer and enjoyer.
• Activities: desire, thought, selection, realisation and understanding.
• Need: happiness; it also feels harmony, trust, respect.
3. The Body
• Material, made of physical elements; acts as the instrument of the Self.
• Activities: eating, breathing, sensing etc.
• Need: physical facility – food, clothing, shelter, etc.
4. Difference
[Basis | Self ('I') | Body]
• Nature | Sentient | Material
• Need | Happiness | Physical facility
• Duration of need | Continuous | Temporary / limited
• Measurable? | No | Yes
5. Interaction and misunderstanding
• The Self and the Body influence each other: if the Self is disturbed, the Body gets ill; if the Body is sick, the Self is disturbed.
• Mistake: we treat the human being as only Body, and try to fulfil all needs with physical facility – which gives pleasure, not happiness.
Conclusion
• Right understanding of the human being as Self + Body is the basis for living in harmony.

unitTitle: Unit 2.0: Relationship, Physical Facility & Human Being
topicTitle: Human Being as Co-existence of the Sentient 'Self' and the Material 'Body'
prompt: Explain harmony of the Self with the Body. Discuss the programme of Sanyam and Swasthya for ensuring it.
modelAnswer:
1. Harmony of Self and Body
• The Self is the master, the Body is the instrument. Harmony exists when the Body acts according to the Self's decision.
• It gives health (Swasthya) and happiness.
2. Sanyam (self-regulation)
• Nurturing – feed the Body with proper food in the right quantity.
• Protection – protect it from harm, weather, disease and bad habits.
• Right utilisation – use the Body for the work that gives mutual happiness (not for self-harm or pleasure only).
3. Swasthya (health)
• The Body is fit and performing its expected function; the Self is in harmony.
• Maintained by proper diet, exercise (asana, pranayama), rest and a positive mind.
4. Programme
• Assess the physical needs correctly.
• Take right quantity of food, hygiene and exercise.
• Avoid over-consumption, addiction, wrong lifestyle.
• Follow a schedule of work, rest and recreation.
Conclusion
• Sanyam and Swasthya ensure that the Body supports the Self in attaining happiness and prosperity.

unitTitle: Unit 3.0: Values in Human Relationships & Society
prompt: Explain the nine values in human-human relationship, with special reference to trust and respect as foundational values.
modelAnswer:
1. Introduction
• Relationship is the connection between two or more people, fulfilled through values. There are nine values: trust, respect, affection, care, guidance, reverence, glory, gratitude, love.
2. The foundational values
• Trust (Vishwas): assurance of right intention in the other (he/she wants me to be happy). Without it, all other values collapse.
• Respect (Samman): right evaluation of the other as a human being, as he/she is – not based on body, wealth, post, age or gender.
3. Other values
• Affection (Sneh): feeling of being related to the other as family.
• Care (Mamta): feeling of responsibility for the nurturing, protection and right utilisation of the body of the other.
• Guidance (Vatsalya): feeling of responsibility for the right understanding and feeling of the other (e.g. parents to children, teachers to students).
• Reverence (Shraddha): acceptance of excellence in the other, in whom I see qualities I wish to attain.
• Glory (Gaurav): feeling of acceptance towards those who have made efforts for the excellence of society.
• Gratitude (Kritagyata): acknowledging the contribution of those who helped my development.
• Love (Prem): feeling of being related to all human beings; the complete value that includes all the above.
4. Respect vs differentiation
• Respect = right evaluation; differentiation = judging by body, wealth, post, age, gender.
• Differentiation leads to discrimination, conflict, disparities in family and society.
5. Importance
• Values make the relationship mutually satisfying and give continuous happiness.
• They are the basis for extending relationship from family to the world family.
Conclusion
• A relationship is fulfilled only when all nine values are understood and lived – starting with trust and respect.

unitTitle: Unit 3.0: Values in Human Relationships & Society
prompt: Explain trust and respect in detail. How do wrong evaluation and differentiation create problems in family and society?
modelAnswer:
1. Trust
• Assurance of the right intention of the other. Every human being wants to be happy and make others happy – this is the natural acceptance.
• We often judge by competence and then doubt the intention – which causes distrust.
• Trust is essential: parent–child, teacher–student, friend–friend, boss–employee.
2. Respect
• Right evaluation of the other as he/she is, and of myself as I am.
• Three types of wrong evaluation: over-evaluation, under-evaluation, otherwise evaluation.
• Respect is for the Self of the person, not for his body or belongings.
3. Problems due to differentiation
• Family: gender and age based discrimination, favouritism, generation gap.
• Society: casteism, racism, communalism, class conflict, corruption.
• Organisation: insecurity, exploitation and low motivation.
4. Solution
• Understand that every human being is the same in intention.
• Evaluate competence separately to improve it, but respect everyone as a human being.
• Practise trust and respect in small daily interactions – family first.
Conclusion
• Trust and respect create a fearless society, the base for the universal human order.

unitTitle: Unit 3.0: Values in Human Relationships & Society
prompt: What is the comprehensive human goal?
modelAnswer:
The comprehensive human goal has four components and covers all levels from the individual to the world:
• Resolution (Samadhan) – individual level: living with right understanding, free from conflict and contradiction.
• Prosperity (Samriddhi) – family level: every family has more than the required physical facility.
• Fearlessness (Abhay) – society level: trust in relationships, no fear of anyone.
• Co-existence (Sah-astitva) – nature / existence level: living in harmony with nature.
• It is achieved through right understanding and a universal human order.

• Universal order (Sarvabhaum Vyavastha): a common system of living acceptable to all, based on human values and natural acceptance.
• Together they form the universal human order – a harmonious world.
• Basis: right understanding + values + mutual fulfilment at all levels.

• Health – Self-regulation (Swasthya–Sanyam): healthy body and responsible living.
• Justice – Preservation (Nyaya–Suraksha): ensuring right relationships and protecting values.
• Production – Work (Utpadan–Karya): producing physical facilities with the right assessment.
• Exchange – Storage (Vinimaya–Kosh): fair exchange and storage of resources.

unitTitle: Unit 3.0: Values in Human Relationships & Society
prompt: Explain the vision of the universal human order – undivided society and universal order – from family to world family.
modelAnswer:
1. Introduction
• Individuals live in families; families form society. Harmony in society is the extension of harmony in the family.
2. Family as the basic unit
• The family is the first place where values are lived: trust, respect, affection, care, guidance, etc.
• The aim of a family is mutual happiness and mutual prosperity among its members.
3. From family to world family
• Families extend to neighbourhood, village, region, nation and the whole world – each time with the same values.
• The feeling of relatedness grows from "my family" to "all human beings are my family".
4. Undivided society and universal order
• Undivided society: relatedness among all humans; no discrimination.
• Universal order: one harmonious system acceptable to all, based on natural acceptance.
5. Comprehensive human goal
• Resolution, prosperity, fearlessness, co-existence at all levels.
6. Five dimensions
• Education–right living, health–self-regulation, justice–preservation, production–work, exchange–storage.
7. Benefits
• No wars or terrorism, trust and fearlessness, proper use of resources, harmony with nature.
Conclusion
• The universal human order is possible if each individual and family lives with right understanding and values.

unitTitle: Unit 3.0: Values in Human Relationships & Society
prompt: Explain the five dimensions of human endeavour in the context of the universal human order.
modelAnswer:
1. Education – Right living

• Present system emphasises only skills – needs to include value education.
2. Health – Self-regulation
• Healthy Body + responsible Self. Sanyam ensures right use of the Body.
3. Justice – Preservation
• Justice = recognition of values and ensuring fulfilment in relationships. Preservation = protection of what is right and of nature.
4. Production – Work
• Producing physical facilities with right assessment of need; avoiding overproduction and exploitation.
5. Exchange – Storage
• Fair exchange of goods and services with mutual benefit, and storing for future needs.
Conclusion
• When all five dimensions work together on the base of values, a harmonious society emerges.

2. Four orders

• Animal | Birds, cattle | Life + desires, instinct

• Soil and water support plants; plants provide food and oxygen to animals and humans; animals provide manure and help seed spread; humans should protect and enrich all.

4. Recyclability and self-regulation

5. Disturbance by humans
• Exploitation, pollution, deforestation, non-biodegradable waste, climate change.
• Humans fail to play their role of enriching and protecting other orders.
6. Solution

• Use recyclable and eco-friendly technology; reduce consumption; take only the needed facility.
Conclusion

• Universal (all humans), continuous (all times), natural (no external pressure), verifiable (by self-exploration).
3. Why it is the basis for ethics
• Ethics based on law or fear can be circumvented; ethics based on natural acceptance is self-driven.
• It ensures consistency – the same standard in family, workplace and society.
• It leads to mutual happiness and removes conflicts of interest.
4. Application in profession
• An engineer who knows that cheating and unsafe design are not naturally acceptable avoids them even without supervision.
• Honesty in reporting, quality, safety and sustainability become natural, not forced.
Conclusion
• Human values, being naturally acceptable, form the most reliable foundation for professional ethics.
